c.tagline: Waffles, art nouveau, and Europe's beating heart.

hood_landmark.Ixelles: the Ixelles Ponds and Flagey square café scene
hood_landmark.Saint-Gilles: the Horta Museum, Victor Horta's Art Nouveau house

hood_landmark.Sablon: the Gothic Church of Our Lady of the Sablon amid famed chocolatiers

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing around Gare du Midi/Nord/Centrale and the metro; caution around the Midi station and Molenbeek at night

hood_desc: Ixelles is a trendy, cosmopolitan and diverse district beloved for its cafes, boutiques and nightlife around Flagey and Chatelain, suits students and young professionals who want a lively, walkable base.
Saint-Gilles is a bohemian and multicultural quarter full of Art Nouveau facades, artist studios and buzzing bars, ideal for creatives and travelers who prefer character over polish.

Marolles is a gritty, authentic working-class neighborhood famous for the Place du Jeu de Balle flea market and cheap eats, a magnet for bargain hunters, antique lovers and those seeking old Brussels grit.
Sablon is an elegant, upscale enclave of antique dealers, chocolatiers and art galleries around a graceful square, best for refined shoppers and visitors wanting a genteel, historic setting.

The European Quarter is a modern business district built around the EU institutions, with glass office towers and an international expat crowd, practical for work trips but noticeably quiet in the evenings and weekends.

The Grand-Place quarter is the Pentagon's tourist core: the UNESCO-listed guildhall square, the Ilot Sacre restaurant lanes, Manneken Pis and the Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert, all within a few minutes' walk of Central Station. It is the most convenient base for a short first visit, and the busiest and priciest part of the city.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though it can be quite hard/chalky.

transit.pay: Tap a contactless bank card, phone or smartwatch directly at metro gates and bus/tram validators, or buy a MOBIB card or ticket through the STIB app, at metro stations, kiosks and vending machines. A single Brupass journey costs about €2.70 (€2.40 tapping a bank card, roughly $2.75-3), and fares auto-cap at about €8.50 per day after four trips.
transit.hours: Metro, tram and bus service runs from about 6am to around midnight, with the Noctis night-bus network taking over on Friday and Saturday nights until roughly 3am.

food.name: Moules-frites
food.desc: A steaming black pot of mussels cooked with white wine, celery or beer, with a cone of fries alongside. Best from September onwards.

places.name: Friture Rene
places.note: Open since 1932, still family-run; reserve ahead, no concessions to tourists.

places.name: Le Zinneke
places.note: Around 69 different mussel preparations, well off the Grand Place trail.

places.name: Chez Leon
places.note: The classic central address since 1893; busy and touristy but consistent.

food.name: Frites
food.desc: Twice-fried in beef fat, served in a paper cone with a sauce of your choice. Order from a fritkot, not a restaurant.

places.name: Maison Antoine
places.note: The most famous fritkot in Belgium; nearby cafes let you eat them with a beer.

places.name: Frit Flagey
places.note: Green kiosk on Place Flagey with queues in every weather; huge sauce selection.

places.name: Fritkot Bompa
places.note: Central and reliable, handy after a beer crawl around Saint-Gery.

food.name: Belgian waffles
food.desc: Two kinds: the light rectangular Brussels waffle with icing sugar, and the dense caramelised Liege waffle sold from street carts.

places.name: Maison Dandoy
places.note: Biscuit house since 1829; the benchmark for both Brussels and Liege waffles.

places.name: Mokafe
places.note: Old-fashioned cafe under the glass arcade roof; waffles with coffee, no queue.

places.name: Gaufres et Waffles
places.note: Central takeaway counter that does a decent hot Liege waffle to walk with.

food.name: Stoofvlees / carbonnade flamande
food.desc: Beef braised for hours in dark Belgian ale with mustard, bread and brown sugar, sweet-sharp and thick. Served with frites.

places.name: Fin de Siecle
places.note: No bookings, no cards traditionally, blackboard menu of Belgian classics; go early.

places.name: Nuetnigenough
places.note: Beer-focused bistro cooking everything with lambic and abbey ales; tiny and popular.

places.name: Restobieres
places.note: Every dish built around a Belgian beer, near the Jeu de Balle flea market.

food.name: Croquettes aux crevettes grises
food.desc: Crisp-fried croquettes packed with tiny North Sea grey shrimp, served with fried parsley and lemon. The Belgian starter.

places.name: Noordzee / Mer du Nord
places.note: Standing-only fish counter on the square; croquettes and shrimp eaten on the street.

places.name: La Belle Maraichere
places.note: Family-run seafood restaurant since 1973, old-school and highly regarded.

places.name: Fin de Siecle
places.note: Generous, unfussy version alongside their stoofvlees and beer list.

food.name: Belgian chocolate and pralines
food.desc: The filled praline was invented in Brussels in 1912. Buy a mixed ballotin and eat the ganaches first.

places.name: Pierre Marcolini
places.note: Bean-to-bar chocolatier with a jewel-box flagship on Place du Grand Sablon.

places.name: Neuhaus
places.note: The original 1857 shop where the praline was invented; still in the same arcade.

places.name: Frederic Blondeel
places.note: Roasts its own beans on site; also does excellent hot chocolate.

food.name: Lambic, gueuze and kriek
food.desc: Spontaneously fermented beers unique to Brussels and the Senne valley: bone-dry gueuze, tart cherry kriek, cloudy young lambic.

places.name: Cantillon Brewery
places.note: Working 1900 lambic brewery and museum; self-guided tour ends with two tastings.

places.name: A la Mort Subite
places.note: Belle Epoque cafe from 1928 with mirrors, waiters in white and its own gueuze.

places.name: Moeder Lambic Fontainas
places.note: Best beer list in the city, with knowledgeable staff and rare lambic on tap.

food.name: Trappist and abbey beer
food.desc: Strong dark ales brewed at monasteries such as Chimay, Orval, Westmalle and Rochefort, each served in its own branded glass.

places.name: Poechenellekelder
places.note: Marionette-filled bar opposite the statue with a deep Trappist and lambic list.

places.name: Delirium Cafe
places.note: Famous for its thousands of beers; loud and touristy, but the range is real.

places.name: Brussels Beer Project
places.note: Modern taproom brewing experimental beers; a contrast to the abbey classics.

landmarks: Grand-Place
A UNESCO World Heritage central square ringed by ornate guildhalls and the Gothic Town Hall, widely considered one of Europe's most beautiful squares.
Atomium
A giant stainless-steel model of an iron crystal built for the 1958 World's Fair, offering futuristic architecture and panoramic city views.
Manneken Pis
The tiny bronze fountain statue of a urinating boy that has become an irreverent, beloved symbol of Brussels' humor.
Royal Palace of Brussels
The official palace of the Belgian monarch, an imposing neoclassical facade that anchors the city's ceremonial heart.
Cathedral of St. Michael and St. Gudula
A twin-towered Gothic cathedral with stunning stained glass, serving as the site of royal weddings and state funerals.
Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert
One of Europe's oldest covered shopping arcades, prized for its elegant glass-vaulted ceiling and classic Belgian chocolate shops.
Mont des Arts
A landscaped terrace and garden linking the lower and upper city, famous for its postcard view over Brussels' rooftops toward the Town Hall spire.
Cinquantenaire Arcade
A monumental triumphal arch set within a grand park, built to mark Belgium's 50th anniversary and now a favorite photo backdrop.
National Basilica of the Sacred Heart
One of the world's largest Art Deco churches, notable for its enormous green dome and sweeping city views from its observation deck.
Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
A leading art museum complex holding masterpieces by Bruegel, Rubens, and Magritte in a stately neoclassical building.

train.note: Nearly all international trains use Brussels-Midi/Zuid; arrive early for Eurostar to London, which has passport and security checks. The Nightjet to Vienna runs three nights a week (Mon/Wed/Fri); European Sleeper's night trains to Prague (via Cologne and Dresden) and Milan (via Zurich, new in 2026) also start here.

bus.note: Most international coaches leave from Brussels-Nord (CCN) or Brussels-Midi. Bring your passport for London-bound buses, which cross the Channel.

ferry.note: Brussels is inland and Belgium currently has no scheduled passenger ferry route. For the UK, take Eurostar, or cross by ferry from Calais or Dunkirk in nearby France (P&O Ferries, DFDS, Irish Ferries to Dover).

half.name: Bruges
half.blurb: Fairytale medieval city laced with canals, cobbled lanes, belfries and step-gabled brick houses.

half.name: Ghent
half.blurb: Lively canal city with medieval towers, a riverside old port and vibrant student energy.

half.name: Antwerp
half.blurb: Stylish port city known for diamonds, fashion, a grand cathedral and Rubens masterpieces.

half.name: Leuven
half.blurb: Compact university town with a dazzling Gothic town hall and centuries-old beer heritage.

half.name: Mechelen
half.blurb: Charming Renaissance city with a towering cathedral, quiet canals and lovely riverside paths.

half.name: Dinant
half.blurb: Dramatic riverside town beneath a clifftop citadel, birthplace of the saxophone.
